FROM A SEASON RECORD TO A WIN CHANCE

Where every number comes from.

Three different things power this model: observed data, relationships fitted to that data, and chosen assumptions. Everything runs in your browser using bundled snapshots; there is no live odds feed.

  1. Read the season record. NBA, MLB and NFL use wins divided by games. NHL uses standings points divided by 2 × games; Premier League uses earned points divided by 3 × matches. Their slider limits are 82 wins, 168 points, 162 wins, 17 wins and 114 points respectively.
  2. Find its place in league history. Compare the win or points percentage with the included team-seasons in that sport. A smoothed historical percentile becomes an internal strength proxy. This translation is a modeling choice: an equally rare NBA and NFL season need not reflect equal true ability.
  3. Turn the strength gap into game odds. NBA and NHL use relationships fitted to past playoff results. The other three sports use illustrative scoring mechanics. Changing the rules can change how much the same strength gap matters.
  4. Play out the format. Calculate scores, ties and best-of-series outcomes. Then sample up to 100,000 matchups. More trials make the simulation steadier; they do not make the assumptions more realistic.
Inspect every sport’s starting numbers

The opportunity counts and scoring-reward mixes are simplified choices, not measured possession/shot/drive datasets. Only NBA and NHL baseline mean scoring here is calculated from the historical snapshots. Their scoring-event probability is derived to match that mean. MLB, NFL and soccer probabilities and means are illustrative.

Inspect the fitted coefficients and other assumptions

Other chosen constants: controlled mechanics use a 0.12 strength coefficient. Game-day form adds −0.24, −0.12, 0, +0.12 or +0.24 to the relative scoring log-odds, with probabilities 6.25%, 25%, 37.5%, 25% and 6.25%. Both are assumptions, not estimated from game-level scoring data.

Default controls: scoring, opportunities, sensitivity and form are 1×; extra event volatility, home advantage and rest edge are 0. The base scoring-event rate is capped at 95% for extreme experiments. Event volatility redistributes rewards to zero/base/double while keeping their mean unchanged. Home and rest sliders are hypothetical log-odds adjustments, not measured points or days.

Format: one game or best of 3/5/7; stop as soon as a team clinches. A fair 50–50 decider resolves every tied score. Games are independent across a series. These are simplifications, including for soccer draws and overtime.

Simulation: 10,000 trials and seed 42 are reproducibility defaults. Headline odds are calculated directly; squares and counts are simulated. The 95% Wilson interval uses the standard 1.96 normal quantile and covers simulation error only. It does not include uncertainty in the fitted coefficients or model design.

Historical outcome checks: NBA and NHL

These checks cover the two fitted leagues. MLB, NFL and Premier League have historical record scales, but their game probabilities have not received equivalent outcome validation.

Observed 2016–2025 playoff rates when the better regular-season record met the worse one: NBA win percentage and NHL standings points percentage. Equal records, play-ins and 2020 NHL preliminary rounds are excluded. These aggregate rates are not forecasts for your selected teams; games within a series are related.

Where does the data come from?

Bundled historical snapshots ground the record sliders: NBA standings and game results from SportsDataverse’s ESPN collection; NHL and MLB records from their official statistics APIs; NFL results from nflverse; and Premier League results from OpenFootball. The sources, sample sizes and exclusions below are part of the model. Nothing loads live while you run an experiment.

LeagueSlider seasonRarity sample
NBA0–82 wins / 82 games240 team-seasons
NHL0–168 points / 84 games (2026–27)250 historical 82-game team-seasons
MLB0–162 wins / 162 games270 team-seasons
NFL0–17 wins / 17 games318 team-seasons (16/17 normalized)
Premier League0–114 points / 38 matches200 team-seasons

The NBA, NHL and Premier League window is 2015–16 through 2024–25; MLB and NFL use 2015–2024. NBA/NHL rarity uses full 82-game seasons, excluding pandemic-shortened seasons. MLB excludes 2020; NFL excludes Buffalo and Cincinnati’s incomplete 2022 schedules. Other MLB 161–163-game seasons are normalized by actual games. This is a fixed historical reference, not every season in league history.

Use the record fans recognize.

NBA, MLB and NFL use season wins. NHL uses standings points: 2 for a win, 1 for an overtime or shootout loss. Premier League uses earned season points: 3 for a win, 1 for a draw. Soccer points are calculated before administrative deductions so the scale reflects on-field results; they can differ from the published table for a penalized club.

NHL’s current 84-game schedule allows 168 points. We compare the selected share of available points against 82-game historical seasons; 100 points today means 100/168, not 100/164. Premier League allows 114 points across 38 matches. Season points describe the record, while both sports’ game-score charts remain in goals.

The rarity readout counts team-seasons at or above that selected pace. Zero examples means “not observed in this sample,” not impossible. Extreme records keep their selected value while the modeled strength is capped.

One matchup. Two sides of the odds.

Team A and Team B each have their own league and season-record slider. Choose a 50-win NBA team and a 10-win NFL team, then choose the rules they both play under. The headline is a direct hypothetical matchup: Team A’s chance to beat Team B and Team B’s chance to beat Team A always total 100%. Changing either record changes both odds.

We translate each source record to relative strength using its historical rarity, then apply the selected sport’s model. This compares hypothetical teams of equivalent standing; it does not model basketball players learning football. Cross-sport translation is an assumption, even when the selected NBA or NHL baseline uses historical game results.

The main probabilities are exact model odds. The outcome grid and win counts come from one shared set of simulated matchups, with Team B winning precisely the trials Team A loses. Ties use a fair decider; regulation ties remain visible. Neutral venues, equal rest and one game are the default.

The alternative rules result keeps both teams fixed and changes the sport, format or context. “Separate benchmark matchups,” under Comparison options, retains the earlier view for saved experiments: each team faces a typical opponent in its own league, and those independent probabilities need not sum to 100%.

Match rarity, or match record percentage.

Historical rarity compares similarly unusual records in each league’s own win or points distribution. Equivalent records can be fractional and are marked ≈; changing the league preserves that translated pace, while moving the slider selects whole wins or points. Record percentage keeps the same fraction of available wins or points: 50% means winning half the games in NBA/MLB/NFL, earning half the available standings points in NHL, or half the available points in Premier League. These are distinct record measures; equal percentages need not imply equally strong seasons.

We interpolate smoothed historical midranks into a latent strength proxy: θ = logit(rank). This gives familiar records a consistent internal scale. Rarity is not itself the chance of winning a matchup, nor proof that teams of equal rarity have equal true ability. Outside the observed range we cap the strength proxy at the nearest observed endpoint and flag the limitation.

How history changes the baseline odds.

For NBA (wins) and NHL (standings points), a regularized logistic fit relates the difference in record-rarity strength to playoff game wins. A separate fitted home term helps avoid assigning the venue effect to record strength. The main simulator starts at neutral venues. We fit all 834 NBA and 870 NHL games in the retained best-of-seven rounds, including equal-record games; equal records are excluded only from the “better record wins” descriptive percentages.

P(home win) = logistic(β × (θhome − θaway) + h × home indicator)

A temporal check trained on 2016–2022 and tested on 2023–2025, with the rank scale built only from training seasons. NBA Brier score was 0.231 versus 0.244 for home advantage alone; NHL was 0.247 versus 0.250. Lower is better. The NHL improvement is small. The shipped model then refits on all ten postseasons. These point estimates do not measure parameter uncertainty; games within a series are dependent.

We translate the fitted neutral game probability into a scoring edge in the event model. Changing scoring, opportunities or variance holds that baseline edge fixed; it does not fit the counterfactual away. Choose Controlled sport mechanics to use the same illustrative skill coefficient in every sport instead. MLB, NFL and Premier League always use illustrative game probabilities, even though their record scales are empirical.

Games are made of opportunities.

Each team gets N independent opportunities, with a chance to produce a scoring reward. NBA and NHL mean scoring levels use the ten-season data (110.26 points and 2.96 actual goals per team-game). Opportunity counts and reward mixtures remain simplified: NBA 100 possessions; NHL 31 shots; MLB 38 batting opportunities; NFL 11 drives; Premier League 12 chances. The fitted baseline does not validate these mechanisms.

edge = baseline skill edge × sensitivity + home + rest + form
pA = logistic(logit(base scoring rate) + edge / 2)
pB = logistic(logit(base scoring rate) − edge / 2)

Home and rest controls are hypothetical event-log-odds adjustments, not fitted real-world days or points. Form is a symmetric five-point game shock. Event volatility adds reward variance while preserving its mean. More points per goal only changes units; more scoring opportunities can change predictability.

Series, draws and simulation uncertainty.

The exact model computes score distributions, then each game’s advancement probability and best-of-series outcome. Seeded Monte Carlo trials sample those game probabilities and stop when one team clinches. Increasing the number of trials reduces simulation noise, not uncertainty about the real world. The 95% interval on the cards measures Monte Carlo error only.

All tied model scores use a fair decider; regulation ties remain visible separately. This is a hypothetical advancement comparison for soccer, not a forecast of league-table wins or actual penalty shootouts. Games are independent across a series. Seeding chooses the extra home game; rest is a fixed scenario edge.

What this leaves out

Opponent schedule strength, player and roster changes, injuries, score-dependent tactics, goalie and pitcher choices, dependence between games, and actual overtime rules. Record rarity contains both skill and luck. A fitted association is not a causal explanation of why the NBA and NHL differ. In the separate-team comparison, the gap bridge first changes Team A’s record to Team B’s, holding the left sport and opponent caliber fixed. It then changes record mapping, the league baseline and scoring mechanics; format and home/rest change separately. Its contributions depend on swap order.

FROM QUESTION TO PRODUCT

Build something
you can explain.

LeagueLab began with a sports argument: why does the stronger team seem to win more reliably in basketball than hockey?

THE AUDIENCE

Curious sports fans

People who want to explore the “why” behind an upset.

THE JOB TO BE DONE

Turn an argument into an experiment

Change one assumption and understand the tradeoff.

THE PRODUCT BET

Understanding through interaction

A controllable model can make probability feel tangible.

Discovery: start with a question

The originating concept was an interactive simulation for a PM portfolio. The scope sharpened from redesigning playoff formats to separating sport mechanics from format effects. The key hypothesis: curious fans want more than a chart of upset rates; they want to see which assumptions drive the difference. This has not yet been validated with user interviews.

The defining product decisions

  1. Familiar records, explicit rarity. Season wins for NBA/MLB/NFL and season points for NHL/Premier League are compared through their own historical distributions. Rarity is a disclosed proxy for ability, not an identity.
  2. Show mechanisms separately. Scoring rate, opportunity count, event variance, and sensitivity belong to the sport layer. Series length, home seed, and rest belong to the format/context layer.
  3. Separate evidence from assumptions. Historical record scales and two playoff fits sit alongside a controlled mechanics mode, with sources, exclusions and a held-out check.
  4. Make the first insight immediate. Start with two familiar season records and one direct matchup, then offer three specific counterfactual experiments.
  5. Keep computation local. A worker prevents simulations from freezing the UI; static hosting keeps cost and operational complexity low.

A deliberate first release

Five sports, two configurable scenarios, seeded runs up to 100,000 trials, controlled comparisons, regulation draw visibility, uncertainty intervals, shareable configuration links, and JSON/CSV exports. No live scores, odds, accounts, real-team rankings, or tournament brackets.

Validation before launch

The repository includes tests for probability normalization, symmetry, compound-event moments, deterministic seeds, reward rescaling invariance, exact best-of-series probabilities, stopping rules, and simulation agreement. Interface checks cover presets, model navigation, export controls, responsive layouts, and stale result handling. These checks validate implementation. A separate temporal NBA/NHL check tests an exploratory record-based predictor; it does not validate the counterfactual mechanisms.

Launch and learn

For a pilot, recruit 5–8 sports fans. Ask them to predict a counterfactual, run it, and explain the result in their own words. Observe where “strength,” “more scoring,” and “confidence interval” cause confusion. All research and success criteria below are proposed, not completed results.

Primary success signal

At least 4 of 5 pilot participants can explain the difference between changing scoring mechanics and changing series length after a five-minute session.

Supporting signals

Time to first experiment, counterfactual completion, successful result explanation, and voluntary sharing. Guardrail: no participant should interpret model probabilities as calibrated real-team predictions.

What comes next

First, improve comprehension from observed usability sessions. Then extend the current NBA/NHL baseline check with rolling temporal splits, series-cluster uncertainty, opponent-adjusted strength and alternative event models. Add real teams or full brackets only if they improve the core learning task. Analytics are intentionally not installed; any future measurement needs an explicit product and privacy decision.
